title: POC Weekly Sync - Quality Eval
summary: Weekly POC sync to review quality evaluation results from the latest prompt set, discuss regressions on recent model changes, re-run scoring with updated guardrails, and align on next steps for benchmark runs and security review. SE proposed prompt tweaks and a scoring rubric update; customer asked for audit log examples and KMS details. Decided to run night-time batch of 500 prompts and compare token-level regressions on Friday.
topics: next steps: benchmark runs and artifact sharing
action_items: Aisha: send updated scoring spreadsheet (includes per-prompt metrics and threshold markers) by 2025-11-14
Marco: run the 500-night batch with current canary model and produce regression diff by 2025-11-14
Priya: share internal golden prompt set (30 examples) and acceptance criteria by 2025-11-13
Danielle: confirm required audit log retention and SSO details by 2025-11-18
next_steps: Run full scoring pass on Friday compare baseline vs canary and share results
Schedule security deep-dive with Arkadia security team next week (SE + Danielle)
Aisha to send pricing for dedicated pilot if regression footprint is acceptable
transcript:
[00:00] Aisha Patel: All right, team, good afternoon — thanks for joining. This is our weekly POC sync for Arcadia. We got about 50 minutes on the calendar. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Sam Turner: Hey everyone, Sam here.
[00:15] Priya Shah: Priya on for eng.
[00:17] Danielle Ortiz: Danielle from security.
[00:19] Leo Nguyen: Leo, data science.
[00:21] Marco Liu: Marco from Redwood SE.
[00:23] Jon Park: Jon, CSM.
[00:25] Aisha Patel: Sweet. Quick agenda: results from last week's quality eval, any regressions, prompt tweaks Marco suggested, and then security questions from Danielle. Sound good?
[00:35] Sam Turner: Yep, let's do it.
[00:38] Marco Liu: Cool, I'll share screen — um, just a heads up the spreadsheet I uploaded has per-prompt accuracy, BLEU-ish style score we used, and severity flags for hallucination. There is a column for token-level cost so you can see latency/cost tradeoffs.
[00:50] Priya Shah: I saw initial notes — curious about the hallucination flag thresholds, those seemed a bit aggressive in a few cases.
[00:58] Marco Liu: Yeah fair — that was set to catch anything with a confidence delta under 0.6 and any freeform entity fallbacks. We can loosen that, I think what matters is the relative regression not the absolute count.
[01:15] Leo Nguyen: One thing we spotted, two prompts in the patient-summarization set regressed pretty badly after the recent canary change — produced extraneous recommendation text.
[01:26] Marco Liu: Right, I have the diff here. Baseline model A produced concise plan, canary B added tertiary recommendation lines referencing procedures that aren't in the notes. Could be an instruction-following drift from the temperature/penalty changes.
[01:40] Aisha Patel: Can you show the exact prompts and responses? We should capture as examples for regression alerts.
[01:45] Marco Liu: Yep. Prompt 12 and 17, I'll paste in the chat. (screenshare noises)
[02:00] [02:00] Marco Liu: Prompt 12 baseline: "Summarize patient visit focusing on med changes and follow-up plan." Baseline response: "Patient..." (truncated) Canary response had extra line: "Recommend cardiology consult for possible X" which is not supported.
[02:20] Sam Turner: Huh, that's not great. Did the canary change the instruction template or the system prompt?
[02:25] Marco Liu: We adjusted the system prompt slightly to favor proactive care suggestions; that was intended to increase helpfulness but it appears to have introduced hallucinations.
[02:34] Priya Shah: This is exactly why we wanted guardrails. Are there guardrail configs we can attach to these sensitive prompt groups?
[02:42] Marco Liu: Yes, guardrails at the route level — you can block output containing certain entity classes or require source citations for clinical recs. We can also set a hard stop on any 'recommendation' token sequence when no supporting evidence exists in the notes.
[02:55] Danielle Ortiz: Can you explain how the evidence check works? We're particularly concerned about false positives and the possibility of blocking valid suggestions. Also need to see audit logs for any blocked outputs.
[03:08] Marco Liu: Sure. Two approaches: 1) lightweight: keyword/entity match vs note contents — cheap and fast; 2) evidence-chain check: run a grounding step that attempts to find supporting spans in the patient note and if none found, either add a citation denial or redact the recommendation. The second is heavier but reduces false positives.
[03:26] Danielle Ortiz: How are these actions logged? We need immutable audit trails with actor IDs and payloads.
[03:32] Jon Park: For POC we can demo logs — we log every request/response along with guardrail decisions, reason codes, and model variant used. We can show a sample log with the canary run.
[03:42] Danielle Ortiz: Retention policy? We have to align with our legal team — minimum 7 years for some artifacts.
[03:48] Aisha Patel: Redwood supports configurable retention, and we integrate with KMS for encrypted at-rest logs. For Private deployments you can set on-prem retention policies. We'll follow up with documented options.
[03:58] Danielle Ortiz: Great, can you share specifics (KMS provider names, HSM support)?
[04:04] Marco Liu: Yes, we support AWS KMS, Google KMS, and customer-managed keys via HSM connectors. I'll put the security doc link in the notes.
[04:13] Priya Shah: Back to scoring: Leo, can you walk us through the metric shifts?
[04:17] Leo Nguyen: Sure — overall macro-score dropped 2.8 points on canary; however most of that came from three prompts in the summarization bucket. If we remove those outliers the drop is under 0.5. Per-token cost increased by ~6% due to longer outputs.
[04:33] Priya Shah: Is longer output acceptable? We have SLA for throughput and latency — more tokens may break our 200ms p50 target on peak.
[04:40] Marco Liu: Good point. We can apply a max token cap per route and prefer more compact system prompt. Also batching changes can help but batching trades latency for throughput.
[04:53] Sam Turner: We're leaning towards hosted for speed of iteration but if cost/latency can't be constrained we may consider dedicated pools. Can the dedicated environment enforce token caps at the router level?
[05:03] Marco Liu: Yes, Dedicated has per-route config including token caps and strict concurrency limits. It's also easier to get predictable p50—though capex is higher.
[05:13] Priya Shah: Any regression detection automation? We don't want to manually inspect diffs every week.
[05:18] Marco Liu: Redwood Optimize includes automatic regression detection on holdout prompt sets and will send alerts when drift exceeds set thresholds. You can configure severity levels (info/warning/critical) and tie them to rollout policies like automatic rollback.
[05:33] Sam Turner: That sounds useful. Could we get a demo of rollback?
[05:36] Aisha Patel: We'll schedule a short demo if you want; Jon can set that up.
[05:40] Jon Park: I'll put a 30-min demo on the calendar next week.
[05:44] Priya Shah: About the scoring rubric — Marco, you mentioned BLEU-ish score, but I think a mix of BLEU, factuality score, and human-labeled severity would be better.
[05:54] Marco Liu: Absolutely. We encourage a hybrid approach: automated metrics for coverage and length, plus a small human-annotated sample for clinical accuracy. We also support custom metrics you can plug in.
[06:06] Leo Nguyen: We'll prepare a 30-sample human eval set and tag severity.
[06:10] Priya Shah: Timelinewise, if we share the gold set by Thursday can Marco's team run the full 500-night batch Friday?
[06:18] Marco Liu: Yes if we get the set by Thursday EOD we can run overnight and have diffs by Friday midday.
[06:24] Sam Turner: On hallucination guardrails, is there a way to degrade gracefully rather than hard-block? e.g., add a disclaimer or ask to confirm.
[06:32] Marco Liu: Totally — you can set soft-block policies that add a "confidence low" footer or return a clarifying question template. Those are less disruptive to UX.
[06:42] Danielle Ortiz: We prefer soft-blocks for user experience but need to track occurrences for audits.
[06:47] Marco Liu: Logs will include action type (soft-block, hard-block), reason code, and link to the evidence check.
[06:55] Priya Shah: Any concerns about PII in logs? We need redaction or tokenization options.
[07:02] Marco Liu: Yep, we have PII redaction pipelines pre-commit; you can configure which fields to redact and what to hash. For Private you can keep raw logs on-prem.
[07:11] Danielle Ortiz: Please include a sample redaction config.
[07:14] Aisha Patel: We'll attach the security pack in the follow-up email.
[07:19] [07:20] Leo Nguyen: Quick note on prompt tuning: Marco suggested changing the instruction to be more constrained by listing allowed recommendation types. That reduced hallucinations in a small A/B test.
[07:32] Marco Liu: Right — adding explicit negative instructions (e.g., "Do not recommend specialty referrals unless present in notes") worked well. But we saw a slight drop in helpfulness metric.
[07:45] Priya Shah: We have to balance helpfulness vs safety. Our acceptance criteria currently: <=1% critical hallucination, <=5% medium hallucination, and p50 latency <200ms.
[07:58] Aisha Patel: Noted. We'll use those thresholds for alerting.
[08:03] Sam Turner: Regarding artifact sharing, what's the easiest way to get the scoring spreadsheet and sample logs?
[08:09] Jon Park: I'll share a secure link (Dropbox/Redwood GH drive) — we'll gate by email.
[08:15] Danielle Ortiz: Make sure access is SSO-protected.
[08:18] Jon Park: Will do.
[08:20] Priya Shah: For the canary rollback policy — if critical regressions >0.5% across clinical prompts, do we auto rollback?
[08:29] Marco Liu: We can set that policy — automatic rollback to the last stable model. We can also pause a rollout and send a human-in-the-loop approval.
[08:37] Sam Turner: Good. On costs — if we throttle token generation to cap tokens, are we charged for the truncated tokens or only for generated tokens?
[08:46] Marco Liu: You're charged for tokens that are generated; if a model is stopped mid-output due to a guardrail, you still incur the tokens produced. But prefix/KV caching can reduce repeated costs for repeated context.
[08:58] Priya Shah: Anything else from the security side Danielle?
[09:02] Danielle Ortiz: Just need the KMS vendor list, HSM options, and sample audit log. Also want to know encryption in transit between Redwood control plane and private deployment.
[09:11] Marco Liu: Encryption in transit uses mTLS and you can provision private endpoints for dedicated/private. We'll include network diagrams.
[09:18] Aisha Patel: OK, quick recap and owners: Marco runs the 500 prompt batch, Aisha sends scoring sheet, Priya shares gold prompts, Danielle confirms retention + KMS details. Jon schedules rollback demo. Anything else?
[09:30] Priya Shah: Could we add a short QA for the canary's system prompt so we know what changed?
[09:34] Marco Liu: I'll attach the exact system prompt diffs in the ticket.
[09:37] Sam Turner: One last note — we want to try a small dedicated pilot if the regression is manageable. Aisha, can you get a ballpark for 3-node dedicated pool?
[09:45] Aisha Patel: Yes, I'll include ballpark pricing in the follow-up.
[09:48] Danielle Ortiz: Thanks everyone.
[09:50] Aisha Patel: Thanks — we'll send notes. End call.
[52:00] (call ended)

Notes: Transcription had occasional mis-hearings — e.g., "KV cache" shows up as "K V cash" in one excerpt. Speaker labels occasionally overlap. Shared artifacts: scoring spreadsheet (link shared in chat), security pack (link to docs), system prompt diffs (ticket #528).
